12398: Household codes (lists of duties for members of a household) appear in Ephesians, Colossians (Col 3:18-4:1) and 1 Peter (1 Pet 2:18-3:7). Their pattern goes back to Aristotle's *Politics* (book 1), which treats the household as made of three pairs (master and slave, husband and wife, father and children) and argues that the male naturally rules. Greek, Roman and Hellenistic Jewish writers (Philo, Josephus) repeated the scheme, often to show that a group was not socially subversive. David Balch argued that early Christians used it partly to defend themselves against charges of undermining households. In the earliest manuscripts of Eph 5:22 there is no verb: 'wives, to your own husbands', borrowing 'submit' from 5:21.
12399: Drunken banquets and the wine-god Dionysus were part of city life; Ephesians contrasts drunken revelry with Spirit-filled singing. In Roman marriage the husband held legal power and wives were expected to show modesty and obedience; husbands were not usually told to love their wives in a self-sacrificing way. Ephesians keeps the expected instruction to wives but reshapes the husband's role around Christ's self-giving death, an expectation with no clear parallel in ancient household codes. 'Head' (kephalē) could mean ruler, source, or the prominent, life-giving part; its sense here is debated.
12400: 'A fragrant offering and sacrifice' (Eph 5:2) uses temple language (Exod 29:18). The light-darkness contrast is strong in the Dead Sea Scrolls (sons of light and sons of darkness). The marriage image of Christ and the church echoes the prophets' picture of God as Israel's husband (Hos 2:19-20, Isa 54:5, Ezek 16:8-14), where the husband washes, clothes and adorns his bride. Gen 2:24, the foundation of Jewish marriage teaching, is read as a picture of the Messiah's union with his people.
12401: Wives heard themselves addressed directly as moral agents who choose their conduct 'as to the Lord', which was unusual. Husbands, the most powerful members of the household, heard the longest and most demanding instructions: a call to self-giving love. A mixed church would hear that their homes were to be small pictures of Christ's love for his people.
12402: The chapter calls Christians to a sexual and economic ethic that refuses exploitation and greed, and to worship that shapes community. How the household code applies today divides complementarians and egalitarians, but both agree it cannot justify domination or abuse, and that 5:21 and 5:25 set the tone.
12403: A pleasing aroma, a food offering to the Lord: Christ's self-giving as sacrifice.
12404: The two become one flesh, quoted in Eph 5:31.
12405: God washes, clothes and adorns his bride Israel.
12406: Arise, shine, for your light has come: possibly echoed in 'Awake, O sleeper... Christ will shine on you'.
12407: Ephesians 5 is mainly about wives submitting to husbands as the head of the home.
12408: The section begins with mutual submission 'to one another' (5:21), addresses wives as free moral agents, and gives husbands the heavier demand: to love as Christ did, by giving himself up. How this shapes roles today is debated, but power used for self-interest is ruled out.
12409: One Master in heaven; standing in God's armour
12410: Children, obey your parents in the Lord; this is the first commandment with a promise. Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger but bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord. Slaves, obey your earthly masters with sincerity, as serving Christ, knowing the Lord will reward whatever good anyone does, slave or free. Masters, do the same to them, stop threatening, knowing that both they and you have the same Master in heaven, and there is no favouritism with him. Finally, be strong in the Lord and put on the whole armour of God to stand against the schemes of the devil, for our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers, authorities, cosmic powers of this darkness and spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. Stand, with the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, feet ready with the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, the word of God, praying at all times in the Spirit. Pray for Paul, an ambassador in chains, and Tychicus will bring news. Peace, love and grace to all who love the Lord Jesus with undying love.
12411: Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world; perhaps a sixth to a third of people in large cities were enslaved or recently freed (estimates vary widely). Slaves could be household managers, teachers or labourers, and had no legal personhood. Ephesians does not call for abolition, which no ancient movement did, but it addresses slaves as moral agents and tells masters they are slaves of the same Lord, who shows no favouritism. Later Christians debated whether such texts endorsed slavery; abolitionists argued their logic undermined it. The imperial cult was strong in Ephesus: a temple to Rome and the deified Julius Caesar was authorised there under Augustus, and a major temple of the emperors (the Sebastoi) was built under Domitian around AD 89-90. Calling Jesus 'Lord' and Paul an 'ambassador' had political overtones.
12412: Roman fathers had legal power (patria potestas) over children, even adult ones; telling fathers not to provoke their children limits that power. Roman soldiers were a familiar sight, and the armour image would be easy to picture, but its content comes from Isaiah. 'Stand' is military language for holding a position against attack. Ancient hearers who feared spirits often wore amulets; Ephesians offers a different protection: being clothed with God's character and word.
12413: 'Honour your father and mother' (Exod 20:12, Deut 5:16) is quoted as still valid for Gentile believers, showing the Torah still teaches them. The armour is drawn from Isaiah: God puts on righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet to bring justice (Isa 59:17); the Messiah wears righteousness and faithfulness as a belt and strikes with the rod of his mouth (Isa 11:4-5); the feet of the herald of peace (Isa 52:7); the servant's mouth like a sharp sword (Isa 49:2). The struggle against rulers and authorities in the heavenly places fits Jewish apocalyptic pictures of battle between God's angels and the powers over the nations (Dan 10:13, Dan 10:20-21). The church now wears the armour of the divine warrior.
12414: Slaves would hear something rare: their work has value before Christ, who will reward them, and their masters are under the same Lord. Children would be addressed directly in the assembly. A small, vulnerable church in a city full of temples and magic would hear that their stand together, in truth, peace and prayer, is part of God's victory.
12415: The household instructions invite reflection on how Christ's lordship reshapes all power relationships, including at work. The armour of God calls the church to stand together by truthfulness, justice, peace-making and prayer, rather than by fear or by technique. Paul asks prayer not for release but for boldness to speak.
12416: The Lord puts on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation.
12417: Righteousness and faithfulness as the belt of the Messiah.
12418: The feet of the messenger who announces peace.
12419: God made the servant's mouth like a sharp sword.
12420: Honour your father and mother, quoted with its promise.
12421: Spiritual warfare means identifying and binding demons, and the armour is a personal prayer routine for protection.
12422: The armour is God's own, from Isaiah, worn by the church together. Its pieces are truth, justice, peace, faith, salvation and God's word, and the command is to stand and pray. The powers are real, but the battle is fought through faithfulness and unity.
12423: Ephesians 1:4-5: election as God pre-selecting individuals only
12424: Before creation God chose certain individuals to be saved and passed over others; Ephesians 1 is mainly about my personal place on that list. (Others react against this and treat election as simply God foreseeing who would choose him.)
12425: The passage is plural and Christ-centred: God 'chose us in him', 'in the Beloved'. In Israel's scriptures election is first of a people (Deut 7:6-8), centred on a chosen representative (Isa 42:1, the servant). William Klein, Markus Barth and N. T. Wright stress corporate election: God chose the Messiah, and a people in him, and anyone joined to him shares that election. The purpose is vocational: 'holy and blameless', 'to the praise of his glory', and the immediate surprise is that Gentiles now share Israel's chosenness (Eph 1:11-14).
12426: Reformed scholars such as Harold Hoehner and Thomas Schreiner argue corporate and individual election are not opposites: a group is made of persons, and 'he chose us... according to the purpose of his will' (Eph 1:11) implies God's choice of those persons. Arminian scholars also accept corporate framing but stress human response. Most agree the text is first about God's gracious initiative and the people in Christ, and that it was meant to produce praise and assurance, not anxiety or debate.
12427: Reading election as corporate and in Christ turns it from a puzzle about who is in or out into a call to be a holy people for the world, and a reason for Gentile believers to know they truly belong.
12429: 'By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.' This is the gospel in a sentence: personal salvation as a free gift received by faith.
12430: The sentence is true and central, but Ephesians does not stop there. Verse 10 says we are God's 'workmanship' (poiēma), created for good works. Verses 11-22 then show what salvation creates: Gentiles once far off brought near, Jew and Gentile made one new humanity, enemies reconciled, a temple for God. Salvation is personal and social at once. Lincoln, Thielman, Cohick and Wright all stress that 2:1-10 and 2:11-22 are two panels of one picture: the same grace that raises the dead creates one people.
12431: Evangelical scholars generally agree; the problem is popular quotation, not scholarly theology. Traditional interpreters add that 'not from works' here is broader than the Jewish boundary markers of Galatians (it is any human doing), which supports the classic Protestant emphasis on grace alone. New Perspective scholars largely accept that point for Ephesians.
12432: A gospel that stops at verse 9 can leave churches content to be collections of saved individuals. Ephesians says the saved are a new community whose unity across hostile lines is itself the evidence of salvation.
12433: Ephesians 5:22 ('Wives, submit') without 5:21 ('submitting to one another')
12434: The household code sets out a chain of command: husbands lead, wives submit, children obey, slaves obey. Submission is a one-way duty owed by those lower in the order.
12435: In the earliest Greek manuscripts 5:22 has no verb of its own; it borrows 'submit' from 5:21, 'submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ', which itself is the last of several results of being filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18-21). The code follows the classic pattern of Aristotle's household management (husband-wife, father-child, master-slave), but reshapes it: wives, children and slaves are addressed as moral agents; husbands are told to love their wives as Christ gave himself up for the church, a demand unheard of in ancient codes; fathers must not provoke their children; masters must stop threatening because they share a Master in heaven. Lynn Cohick and Craig Keener emphasise this counter-cultural reshaping.
12436: Complementarian scholars (such as Thielman, Hoehner and Schreiner in other writings) agree that 5:21 governs the passage and that husbands' headship must be self-giving, but argue that mutual submission does not erase distinct roles: 'one another' can mean 'some to others' in their appropriate relationships, and the code still asks wives to submit to husbands. Egalitarian scholars argue that the code was a missionary accommodation to its culture, like its instructions to slaves, and that its inner logic points beyond it. Both reject using the passage to justify abuse.
12437: Read without 5:21 and 5:25, the code can be used to defend domination; read whole, it subordinates every household power to Christ's self-giving love. How it applies today remains debated.
12438: Ephesians 6:12: spiritual warfare as a private hunt for demons
12439: Because 'we wrestle not against flesh and blood', Christians should identify and cast out territorial spirits, bind demons in prayer, and see spiritual attack behind most personal troubles.
12440: Ephesians does take the powers seriously; Clinton Arnold shows that its hearers in a city full of magic needed to know Christ rules over them. But the commands are to 'stand' (four times), to put on the armour (mostly virtues: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the word of God) and to pray, including for Paul's preaching. The 'you' is plural: the church stands together. The struggle shows up concretely in lies, anger, theft, sexual exploitation and division (Eph 4:25-31): 'do not give the devil a foothold' (Eph 4:27) comes in a passage about anger. Walter Wink argues the powers are also the spirituality of institutions and systems.
12441: Many charismatic and Pentecostal scholars, and Arnold himself, argue the passage assumes real personal spiritual beings and that prayer against them is appropriate; deliverance ministry has New Testament precedent (Acts 16:18, Acts 19:11-12). Critics of Wink say he reduces personal beings to social structures. A shared middle ground: the powers are real, the believer's main weapons are faithfulness, unity, truth and prayer, and Christ has already won.
12442: Spiritual warfare in Ephesians looks like a united church telling the truth, refusing hatred and proclaiming peace, not like anxious hunting for demons behind every event.
12443: 'Heavenly places' as escape from the world
12444: Believers are seated with Christ in the heavenly places (Eph 2:6), so our real home is up in heaven; the goal of faith is to rise above earthly concerns until we go there.
12445: 'The heavenly places' (ta epourania) in Ephesians is the unseen realm where the powers operate too (Eph 3:10, Eph 6:12). Being seated with Christ there means sharing his authority now, in this world. God's plan is to unite 'all things in heaven and on earth' (Eph 1:10), and the letter's second half is intensely earthly: work, speech, marriage, slaves and masters. Andrew Lincoln and N. T. Wright stress that heaven and earth are being brought together, not separated.
12446: Traditional interpreters agree the phrase is not escapist; they emphasise the believer's present spiritual blessing and secure position, and the future hope of glory (Eph 1:14, Eph 1:18). The difference is mainly emphasis.
12447: If heaven is an escape hatch, the church withdraws; if heaven and earth are being united in Christ, the church becomes a foretaste of that union in ordinary life.
12448: Abolishing 'the law of commandments' means the church replaces Israel
12449: Ephesians 2:15 says Christ abolished the law, so Israel's covenants are over and the church is the new, non-Jewish people of God.
12450: Ephesians says the opposite of Gentile replacement: Gentiles are brought into what Israel already had: the commonwealth of Israel, the covenants of promise, hope and God (Eph 2:12, Eph 2:19). What is abolished is the law 'of commandments in ordinances' as a dividing wall of hostility between the two (Eph 2:14-15), the way it functioned to separate. Markus Barth and, from a Messianic Jewish angle, Mark Kinzer argue that the 'one new humanity' unites two peoples without erasing Jewish identity, rather like a marriage.
12451: Many evangelical scholars (Hoehner, Thielman) argue that the new humanity is a genuinely new entity, 'neither Jew nor Gentile' in its basis, and that the Mosaic law no longer governs the people of God. They still reject contempt for Jews and describe Gentiles joining Israel's hope, not stealing it.
12452: This shapes Christian attitudes to the Jewish people: Gentile Christians are guests grafted into Israel's story, not its replacements.
12453: The armour of God as a solo soldier's equipment
12454: Each morning I put on the armour piece by piece in prayer to protect myself from attack.
12455: The armour is first God's own: in Isa 59:17 the Lord puts on righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet to rescue his people; in Isa 11:5 the Messiah wears righteousness and faithfulness as a belt; Isa 52:7 gives the feet of the messenger of peace. Ephesians clothes the church, together (plural 'you'), with God's own character and mission. The image may also draw on the Roman soldier, but the content is Isaiah.
12456: Devotional use of the armour is not wrong; scholars across traditions affirm personal appropriation. The correction is that the armour is communal, defensive ('stand'), and made of virtues and the gospel rather than techniques.
12457: The church wins by being like God, truthful, just and peace-bringing, together, not by individual spiritual technique.
12459: John Calvin; Harold Hoehner (2002), Frank Thielman (2010), Clinton Arnold (2010), Peter O'Brien
12460: Ephesians is by Paul. It teaches God's sovereign election of individuals in Christ, salvation by grace alone through faith alone apart from any works, Christ's cosmic victory, and the church as his body. The Jew-Gentile union is a fruit of reconciliation to God.
12461: Takes the letter's language of grace and divine initiative at full strength; strong exegetical commentaries defending authorship and unity.
12462: Can treat 2:11-22 as an application rather than the climax of chapter 2, and can individualise election. Defenders reply that the vertical reconciliation (to God) grounds the horizontal (to each other), as 2:16 itself says.
12464: N. T. Wright, James D. G. Dunn, Scot McKnight
12465: Ephesians shows the goal of Paul's gospel: the single family promised to Abraham, Jew and Gentile together, as the sign to the powers that God's new creation has begun. 'Not by works' in Ephesians broadens Galatians' debate over the law into a general principle, which Dunn and others see as a development within the Pauline tradition.
12466: Makes the Jew-Gentile union central, as the letter does; links election, temple and mystery to Israel's story.
12467: Traditional critics fear it downplays personal sin and forgiveness (Eph 1:7, Eph 2:1-3). Wright responds that both are central and inseparable.
12469: Mark S. Kinzer, Markus Barth; related to Paul within Judaism scholars
12470: The 'one new humanity' is a union of two distinct peoples, Jews who may continue in covenant practice and Gentiles who join Israel's God without becoming Jews. Gentiles are brought into the commonwealth of Israel, not the other way round.
12471: Honours Eph 2:12 and 2:19 and the ongoing place of the Jewish people; resists supersessionism.
12472: Critics argue 2:15 ('abolishing the law of commandments') and 'one new humanity' imply the end of the law's distinctive role for Jewish believers too. Defenders reply that what ends is the law's role as a wall of hostility, not Jewish identity.
12474: Clinton Arnold (*Ephesians: Power and Magic*, 1989), Walter Wink (*Naming the Powers*, 1984), Timothy Gombis (*The Drama of Ephesians*, 2010), Michael Heiser
12475: The letter is a drama of divine warfare: God in Christ triumphs over the rebellious powers and displays that victory in a united church. Arnold reads it against Ephesian magic and the fear of spirits; Wink reads the powers as including the inner spirit of institutions; Heiser reads them against the Old Testament divine council.
12476: Explains the letter's frequent 'powers' vocabulary and its cosmic scope; speaks to people in cultures that fear spirits.
12477: Readings can tilt either toward demythologising (Wink) or toward speculative demonology; the divine-council framework is debated. Each side reminds the other that the text affirms both personal powers and their effects in human structures.
12479: Andrew Lincoln (Word Biblical Commentary, 1990), Ernest Best (1998), Margaret MacDonald (2000)
12480: A disciple of Paul wrote Ephesians, perhaps around AD 80-90, using Colossians as a model, to summarise Paul's legacy for Gentile churches in a later generation. The church is now a universal body, and future hope is more 'realised' (believers already raised and seated with Christ).
12481: Accounts for differences in style, vocabulary, church concept and the close parallels with Colossians; most such scholars treat the letter as valuable and inspired-in-tradition.
12482: Defenders of Pauline authorship (Hoehner, Thielman, Arnold, Cohick) note that ancient writers varied style by genre and secretary, that ancient churches never doubted it, and that Paul's ideas elsewhere already include cosmic Christ and a universal church. Hoehner's survey found scholarly opinion roughly evenly divided.
12484: God picked particular individuals for heaven.
12485: God chose a people 'in him', the Messiah, for holiness and praise, as he chose Israel. Debated how corporate and individual election relate.
12487: Fixing each person's eternal destiny in advance.
12488: Marking out beforehand a destiny: here, adoption as sons and the inheritance. The focus is on the goal God set for his people in Christ.
12491: A divine secret now revealed, as in Daniel's Aramaic raz: God's plan to unite all things in Christ and make Gentiles fellow heirs.
12494: To gather everything under one head: God's plan to bring heaven and earth together in the Messiah.
12497: The unseen realm where Christ reigns, believers share his position, and hostile powers still operate.
12500: Spiritual powers behind nations and systems, in Jewish thought often linked to heavenly beings set over nations (Deut 32:8-9) who rebelled. They can also work through human structures.
12502: A general barrier between God and people.
12503: The wall of separation between Jew and Gentile, probably evoking the temple barrier whose inscriptions warned Gentiles not to pass on pain of death, and the law's role in dividing.
12506: The assembled people of God; in Greek cities the citizen assembly, and in the Greek Old Testament Israel gathered before God. In Ephesians, the whole body of Christ across places.
12509: Debated: 'authority over' or 'source' or the one who gives life and unity to the body. In Ephesians Christ as head both rules and nourishes the body (Eph 4:15-16, Eph 5:23-29).
12512: To place oneself in order under another; in 5:21 it is mutual, flowing from the Spirit and reverence for Christ. Its relation to roles is debated.
12515: The complete equipment of a soldier, filled with the content of God's own armour in Isaiah: truth, justice, peace, faithfulness, salvation and his word.
12518: The management of a household. God is the householder administering his plan for the fullness of time, and Paul is a steward of it.
